source: This suggests that inhibition of transgene expression is reversible at intermediate ML336 concentrations, while sustained replicase inhibition at higher concentrations leads to irreversible replicon loss and permanent termination of transgene expression.

claim: Prolonged ML336 exposure did not compromise cell viability relative to mock-transfected controls.

claim: eIF4E phosphorylation is a key regulator of cell growth and proliferation.
source: This difference may reflect altered cell proliferation over the course of the experiment, consistent with our earlier finding that saRNA reduces eIF4E phosphorylation (Figure 3c), a key regulator of cell growth and proliferation (Muta et al., 2011).

claim: saRNA-induced translation shutdown is thought to be mediated by phosphorylation of eIF2α.
source: saRNA-induced translation shutdown is thought to be mediated by phosphorylation of eIF2α (Beissert et al., 2017; Frolova et al., 2023; Minnaert et al., 2021), following the activation of PKR in response to dsRNA replicative intermediates (Gorchakov et al., 2004; Beissert et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Beissert et al., 2017; Frolova et al., 2023; Minnaert et al., 2021.

claim: saRNA reduces eIF4E phosphorylation, a phenomenon previously observed with alphavirus replicons.
source: Our findings support this model and further show that saRNA reduces eIF4E phosphorylation, a phenomenon previously observed with alphavirus replicons, though its mechanism remains unclear (Berglund et al., 2007; Fros and Pijlman, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript and citations to Berglund et al., 2007; Fros and Pijlman, 2016.

claim: Reduced eIF4E phosphorylation suppresses cap-dependent translation initiation.
source: Reduced eIF4E phosphorylation suppresses cap-dependent translation initiation (Scheper and Proud, 2002), thereby favoring cap-independent translation (Dyer et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Scheper and Proud, 2002; Dyer et al., 2003.

claim: Reduced eIF4E phosphorylation favors cap-independent translation.
source: Reduced eIF4E phosphorylation suppresses cap-dependent translation initiation (Scheper and Proud, 2002), thereby favoring cap-independent translation (Dyer et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dyer et al., 2003.

claim: eIF2α phosphorylation and reduced eIF4E activity likely explain why IRES-driven transgenes achieve higher expression than their cap-dependent counterparts when using conventional saRNA.
source: Together, eIF2α phosphorylation and reduced eIF4E activity likely explain why IRES-driven transgenes achieve higher expression than their cap-dependent counterparts when using conventional saRNA (Erasmus et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and citations to Erasmus et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2022.

claim: Many viruses exploit host shutoff as a strategy to redirect cellular resources toward their replication.
source: Many viruses exploit host shutoff—the global suppression of host gene expression—as a strategy to redirect cellular resources toward their replication (Gaucherand and Gaglia, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gaucherand and Gaglia, 2022.

claim: saRNA co-opts the host shutoff mechanism.
source: Our study suggests that saRNA also co-opts this mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing RNase L activation and host mRNA degradation.

claim: RNase L activation degrades host mRNAs without impairing the translation machinery.
source: RNase L activation then degrades host mRNAs without impairing the translation machinery (Donovan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Donovan et al., 2017.

claim: saRNA transcripts are largely protected from degradation due to their localization within viral replication organelles known as spherules.
source: saRNA transcripts, on the other hand, are largely protected from degradation due to their localization within viral replication organelles known as spherules (Pietilä et al., 2017; Minnaert et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pietilä et al., 2017; Minnaert et al., 2021.

claim: The cleaving of actively translated mRNAs leads to ribosome stalling at 3' ends and ribosome collisions.
source: The cleaving of actively translated mRNAs leads to ribosome stalling at 3' ends and ribosome collisions (Guydosh et al., 2017; Xi et al., 2024), activation of the ribotoxic stress response (Snieckute et al., 2022), and ultimately, apoptosis (Li et al., 2004; Xi et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Guydosh et al., 2017; Xi et al., 2024.

claim: Ribosome stalling and collisions activate the ribotoxic stress response.
source: The cleaving of actively translated mRNAs leads to ribosome stalling at 3' ends and ribosome collisions (Guydosh et al., 2017; Xi et al., 2024), activation of the ribotoxic stress response (Snieckute et al., 2022), and ultimately, apoptosis (Li et al., 2004; Xi et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Snieckute et al., 2022.

claim: The ribotoxic stress response ultimately leads to apoptosis.
source: The cleaving of actively translated mRNAs leads to ribosome stalling at 3' ends and ribosome collisions (Guydosh et al., 2017; Xi et al., 2024), activation of the ribotoxic stress response (Snieckute et al., 2022), and ultimately, apoptosis (Li et al., 2004; Xi et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2004; Xi et al., 2024.

claim: PKR is a central mediator of apoptosis in response to cytosolic dsRNA.
source: Many additional studies further support PKR as a central mediator of apoptosis in response to cytosolic dsRNA (Xu et al., 2018; Gil and Esteban, 2000; Zhang and Samuel, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Xu et al., 2018; Gil and Esteban, 2000; Zhang and Samuel, 2007.

claim: Apoptosis mediated by PKR can occur independently of eIF2α phosphorylation.
source: Notably, apotosis mediated by PKR can occur independently of eIF2α phosphorylation (von Roretz and Gallouzi, 2010), suggesting that inhibiting PKR may not fully prevent its cytotoxic actions.
evidence: This is supported by citation to von Roretz and Gallouzi, 2010.

claim: The E3 construct may be particularly well suited for immunotherapeutic applications such as vaccines or oncolytic-like therapies.
source: This dual-edged effect may make the E3 construct particularly well suited for immunotherapeutic applications such as vaccines or oncolytic-like therapies, where robust transgene expression and immunogenic cell death are advantageous (Leitner et al., 2004; Wu et al., 2023).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and citations to Leitner et al., 2004; Wu et al., 2023.

claim: dsRNA activates NF-κB even in the absence of PKR and RNase L.
source: This agrees with prior reports showing that dsRNA activates NF-κB even in the absence of PKR and RNase L (Iordanov et al., 2001), suggesting that alternative pathways contribute to NF-κB activation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Iordanov et al., 2001.

claim: Reduced eIF4E phosphorylation decreases the levels of the short-lived IκBα protein.
source: Reduced eIF4E phosphorylation has been shown to decrease the levels of the short-lived IκBα protein (Herdy et al., 2012), an inhibitor of NF-κB that sequesters it in the cytoplasm and prevents nuclear translocation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Herdy et al., 2012.

claim: IκBα is an inhibitor of NF-κB that sequesters it in the cytoplasm and prevents nuclear translocation.
source: Reduced eIF4E phosphorylation has been shown to decrease the levels of the short-lived IκBα protein (Herdy et al., 2012), an inhibitor of NF-κB that sequesters it in the cytoplasm and prevents nuclear translocation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IκBα.

claim: Decreased IκBα levels allow NF-κB to translocate to the nucleus, initiating cytokine expression and inflammatory responses.
source: Decreased IκBα levels thus allow NF-κB to translocate to the nucleus, initiating cytokine expression and inflammatory responses (Liu et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2017b and is established knowledge.

claim: NF-κB is best known for promoting inflammatory cytokine production.
source: Importantly, while NF-κB is best known for promoting inflammatory cytokine production, it also supports cell survival by inducing anti-apoptotic genes, though its effects vary by tissue type and biological context (Luo et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Luo et al., 2005 and is established knowledge.

claim: NF-κB supports cell survival by inducing anti-apoptotic genes.
source: Importantly, while NF-κB is best known for promoting inflammatory cytokine production, it also supports cell survival by inducing anti-apoptotic genes, though its effects vary by tissue type and biological context (Luo et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Luo et al., 2005.

claim: In FLS, overexpression of srIκBα reduces cytokine production but increases sensitivity to TNF-induced apoptosis.
source: In FLS, overexpression of srIκBα reduces cytokine production but increases sensitivity to TNF-induced apoptosis (Miagkov et al., 1998; Zhang et al., 2000), consistent with our findings that saRNA encoding srIκBα lowered both cytokine responses and cell viability.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Miagkov et al., 1998; Zhang et al., 2000.

claim: NF-κB inhibition with srIκBα renders liver hepatocytes more susceptible to pro-apoptotic stimuli.
source: This phenomenon is not unique to FLS; NF-κB inhibition with srIκBα also renders liver hepatocytes more susceptible to pro-apoptotic stimuli (Xu et al., 1998), raising safety concerns given that RNA delivery systems such as lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) tend to accumulate in the liver (Sago et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Xu et al., 1998; Sago et al., 2019.

claim: RNA delivery systems such as lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) tend to accumulate in the liver.
source: This phenomenon is not unique to FLS; NF-κB inhibition with srIκBα also renders liver hepatocytes more susceptible to pro-apoptotic stimuli (Xu et al., 1998), raising safety concerns given that RNA delivery systems such as lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) tend to accumulate in the liver (Sago et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sago et al., 2019.

claim: Smad7 can inhibit TGF-β-induced apoptosis.
source: Smad7 can inhibit TGF-β-induced apoptosis (Patil et al., 2000; Yamamura et al., 2000), while SOCS1 can suppress apoptosis triggered by IFN-α, IFN-β (Zitzmann et al., 2007), IFN-γ (Mann-Chandler et al., 2005), and TNF-α (Yan et al., 2008; Madonna et al., 2012; Kimura et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Patil et al., 2000; Yamamura et al., 2000.

claim: SOCS1 can suppress apoptosis triggered by IFN-α, IFN-β, IFN-γ, and TNF-α.
source: Smad7 can inhibit TGF-β-induced apoptosis (Patil et al., 2000; Yamamura et al., 2000), while SOCS1 can suppress apoptosis triggered by IFN-α, IFN-β (Zitzmann et al., 2007), IFN-γ (Mann-Chandler et al., 2005), and TNF-α (Yan et al., 2008; Madonna et al., 2012; Kimura et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zitzmann et al., 2007; Mann-Chandler et al., 2005; Yan et al., 2008; Madonna et al., 2012; Kimura et al., 2004.

source: These anti-apoptotic effects likely enable Smad7 and SOCS1 to mitigate srIκBα-induced reductions in FLS cell viability.

claim: Ruxolitinib is a small-molecule inhibitor of Janus kinase (JAK) 1 and JAK2.
source: This hypothesis is supported by previous studies showing that ruxolitinib—a small-molecule inhibitor of Janus kinase (JAK) 1 and JAK2 (Goker Bagca and Biray Avci, 2020)—increases saRNA transgene expression when added to saRNA polyplexes (Blakney et al., 2021b).

claim: Ruxolitinib increases saRNA transgene expression when added to saRNA polyplexes.

evidence: This is supported by citation to Blakney et al., 2021b.

claim: SOCS1 is an endogenous inhibitor of JAK1 and JAK2.
source: As SOCS1 is an endogenous inhibitor of JAK1 and JAK2 (Liau et al., 2018), it offers a genetically encoded alternative to the small-molecule approach of ruxolitinib for enhancing saRNA-driven transgene expression.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liau et al., 2018.

source: Both preclinical and clinical data indicate that saRNA vaccines often trigger an intense innate immune response, which can hinder antigen expression (Dominguez et al., 2023; Blakney et al., 2021b; Beissert et al., 2017).
